processing_steps.method: vacuum induction melting in Al2O3 crucibles with solidification in Cu moulds
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Binary Fe-Al alloys prepared from Fe of 99.99% purity (purified by zone melting) and Al of 99.999% purity, solidified in Cu moulds to rods usually 18 mm diameter; the as-cast material was used without any subsequent heat treatment. This as-cast state is the baseline for the composition-dependent yield-stress and ductility study.

structures.overall_structure: Polycrystalline as-cast alloy with a coarse grain structure; grain sizes of the order of 1 mm; the as-cast state contained no second phases.

phases_present.phase_name: Fe-Al solid solution (single phase; no second phases in as-cast state)

structures.overall_structure: Dislocation substructure of the quenched Fe-12%Al (60 ppm C) alloy after 5.5% compressive straining: inhomogeneous, with dense dark glide bands of tangled dislocations separating lighter regions that contain isolated long straight dislocations. Before deformation only few straight dislocations were observed in the quenched alloy.

defects.type: dislocations: glide bands with dislocation tangles between them; few straight dislocations before deformation

structures.overall_structure: Dislocation substructure of the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al (60 ppm C) alloy after 5.5% compressive straining: a well-developed dislocation cell structure with thick dark cell walls of high dislocation density enclosing lighter, nearly dislocation-free cell interiors (cell dimensions comparable to or smaller than the 0.4 µm scale bar). Before deformation nearly no dislocations were observed in the furnace-cooled alloy.

defects.type: dislocations: well-developed dislocation cell structure (thick cell walls enclosing nearly dislocation-free interiors); nearly no dislocations before deformation

interfaces.phase_evolution: In the as-cast state the alloy contained no second phases. Fine thin platelike or rod-like precipitates, believed to be carbides (due to the presence of carbon), form on grain boundaries after slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C or prolonged heat treatments (e.g. 14 days at 320 °C); the amount of these grain-boundary particles decreases with lower C content.
interfaces.interface_notes: The Fe-12%Al alloy contains 50–60 wt.ppm C and 60–90 wt.ppm Si; grain-boundary carbide precipitation is therefore expected upon slow cooling.

measurement_conditions.environment: compression test (0.2% proof stress, total straining at least 5%)
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al alloys (Table 1); usually two specimens per alloy tested, yield stress data differ by 3% at most. Yield stress increases linearly with increasing Al content up to 18 at.% with a hardening coefficient of about 2.2 GPa (interpolating lines give 21 and 23 MPa per unit% Al for the higher rate and the lower rate, respectively). Individual value for Fe-12%Al is not reported numerically.

measurement_conditions.strain_rate: 10^-4 s^-1 (tension rate in Figs 4, 5); general range 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^-2 s^-1
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: cylindrical specimens prepared by turning per DIN 50125
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al alloys (Table 1); data averaged over 3–4 tests with yield stress and strength data differing by 3% at most. Yield stress in tension equals that in compression at same rate and temperature. At -100 °C the yield stress and ultimate tensile strength are higher than at room temperature by about 80 MPa. Ductility (strain before necking and fracture strain) decreases with increasing Al content; both show apparent relative maxima at about 8 and 12 at.% Al at room temperature. Individual values for Fe-12%Al are not reported numerically.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Philips CM20 instrument with 200 kV; thin foils prepared by electrolytic twin jet polishing at -30 °C and 12 V voltage using a 7:3 mixture of methanol and nitric acid, with ion milling applied if necessary
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Fe-12%Al (60 ppm C) specimens quenched or furnace-cooled from 1100 °C and deformed by 5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 at room temperature
characterization_methods.purpose: Study the dislocation distribution after deformation of quenched vs furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al (60 ppm C)
characterization_methods.key_findings: Quenched alloy: dense glide bands with dislocation tangles between them, with isolated long straight dislocations between bands; only few straight dislocations before deformation. Furnace-cooled alloy: deformation initiates a dislocation cell structure with thick cell walls and nearly dislocation-free interiors; nearly no dislocations before deformation. The cell formation (requiring sufficient dislocation mobility) occurs only in the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al, indicating that quenching reduces dislocation mobility (attributed to excess vacancies) and that Fe-12%Al shows only a weak effect of quenching.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Specimens etched by an alcoholic 10% nitric acid solution
characterization_methods.key_findings: Coarse grain structure with grain sizes of the order of 1 mm; the as-cast alloys contained no second phases.

characterization_methods.technique: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray analysis (EDX)
characterization_methods.purpose: Study fracture surfaces and perform qualitative precipitate analysis
characterization_methods.key_findings: Used for fracture-surface examination and qualitative precipitate analysis of the Fe-Al alloys.
Real Al content of the nominal Fe-12 alloy is 12.0 at.% (6.2 wt.-%).

unmapped_findings: Composition of the Fe-12%Al alloy (Table 1, nominal 12): real Al 12.0 at.% (6.2 wt.-%); impurities C 50–60 wt.ppm, Si 60–90 wt.ppm, Cu <40 wt.ppm.

The Fe-12%Al alloy (with 60 ppm C) showed only a weak effect of quenching; distinct dislocation cell formation (requiring sufficient dislocation mobility) after deformation was observed only in the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al alloy, whereas the quenched alloy deformed by planar glide with tangles only (Fig. 6).

For the polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al alloys (including Fe-12%Al) the yield stress increases linearly with increasing Al content up to 18 at.% with a hardening coefficient of about 2.2 GPa (interpolating lines: 21 and 23 MPa per unit% Al for the 10^-2 s^-1 and 10^-4 s^-1 rates, respectively); this is not sensitive to deformation rate or temperature and is attributed to Suzuki's solid-solution hardening theory for bcc alloys.
At -100 °C the yield stress and ultimate tensile strength values of the as-cast polycrystalline Fe-Al alloys are higher than at room temperature by about 80 MPa.

Ductility, characterised by strain before necking and fracture strain, decreases with increasing Al content; both strains show apparent relative maxima at about 8 and 12 at.% Al at room temperature (less pronounced at -100 °C).
The Fe-12%Al alloy is a polycrystalline as-cast alloy with grain sizes of the order of 1 mm, used for the TEM dislocation-structure comparison of quenched vs furnace-cooled states.
